newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament avoids clash over budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament avoids clash over budget cuts.

text.p: The Russian parliament ducked out of a clash with the government over spending cuts on Wednesday by rejecting a plan to double money supply.

But it looked set to delay a decision on the government's budget squeeze for a second time, dragging out a battle of wills between the communist deputies who dominate the State Duma, or lower house, and the liberal reformers who hold sway in the cabinet.
Ministers say spending cuts are unavoidable because of huge shortfalls in tax revenue. But deputies are appalled, saying the cuts will make life even harder for the struggling majority of Russians.
Some of the communist deputies and their allies who dominate the chamber said Russia should print money instead of cutting spending by about a fifth as the government proposes.
But the Duma, scared by oblique threats of dissolution from the government, which is backed by President Boris Yeltsin, rejected that proposal on Wednesday.
It also threw out a proposal to strike the clause from the budget law under which the government must seek parliament's approval for any spending cuts.

The aim of that suggestion was to lay the blame squarely with the government for the social consequences of the cuts, and to ensure that spending is reduced equally across the board in line with the existing budget.

Instead, deputies accepted in principle a suggestion that they look into exactly where the cuts would fall. They were due to vote again on the proposal later in the afternoon, but cannot change it substantially.
It includes creating a commission from representatives of the two houses of parliament and the government, with the task of presenting proposals by June 18.
In theory, this will give the Duma enough time to make a final decision on the spending cuts before it breaks up for its summer recess, now put off until June 24.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, in charge of the government while Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is on vacation, has urged deputies to approve the cuts and the first reading of a new tax code before their summer break.
The tax code, which aims to make Russia's convoluted tax system more workable and transparent, has already become the basis for the government's 1998 budget draft.
Parliament had put off a decision on the cuts once before, asking the government last month to detail how it would boost revenues for the rest of the year.
The government said it would exert pressure on Russia's major tax debtors, such as the Gazprom gas monopoly, car maker AvtoVaz, and oil firms Sibneft and Nizhnevartovskneftegaz.
Budget revenues were just 65 percent of the target in the first four months of the this year.
The government has already cut spending at its own discretion by 70 percent of budgeted levels, but presented an official plan to reduce 1997 outgoings by 108 trillion roubles ($18.8 billion).
It is also proposing to raise budgeted revenues by 30 trillion roubles, mainly through privatisation and on securities markets.

Chubais declined an invitation to address the Duma on Wednesday. He has said the government will go ahead with its plans regardless of parliament's decision, but nevertheless wants to see his plans approved.

"The formal legalisation of the rejigged budget is very important to the pedants from international financial organisations; they prefer to lend money to a government working with a judicially solid budget," the Obshchaya Gazeta weekly said.
($ = 5,760 Russian Roubles)
